source_refs.note: Book p. 103-107: area under a curve, Notes 1-5, signed and net signed area, Examples 57-59 with Figures 3.1-3.7

blocks.text: A remarkable result in calculus is that the area under the graph of \(y = f(x)\), where \(f(x) \ge 0\), can be obtained simply by evaluating the definite integral of \(f(x)\) over the interval \([a, b]\).
If \(f\) is continuous and \(f(x) \ge 0\) over the interval \([a, b]\), then the area \(A\) of the region under the curve of \(f\) from \(a\) to \(b\) is

blocks.text_alt: A equals the integral from a to b of f of x d x

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does an integral give an area? Cut the region into very thin vertical strips. A strip at position \(x\) has width \(dx\) and height \(f(x)\), so its area is about \(f(x)\,dx\). Adding all strips from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\) and letting the width shrink to zero is exactly what \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) means.
When to use it: the region is bounded above by the curve, below by the \(x\)-axis, and on the sides by \(x = a\) and \(x = b\), with the curve on or above the axis.
Notes

1. If \(f(x) \le 0\) on the interval \([a, b]\), then the area bounded by the curve \(y = f(x)\) and the \(x\)-axis is given by \(\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\right|\), or equivalently \(\int_a^b |f(x)|\,dx\), or equivalently \(-\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).

blocks.alt: A curve y = f(x) lying below the x-axis between the vertical lines x = a and x = b; the region between the curve and the axis is shaded.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.1: f(x) ≤ 0 on [a, b] (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: 2. If \(f(x) \ge 0\) on the interval \([a, c]\) and \(f(x) \le 0\) on the interval \([c, b]\), then the total area bounded by the curve \(y = f(x)\) and \(x\)-axis on the interval \([a, b]\) is \(\int_a^c f(x)\,dx + \left|\int_c^b f(x)\,dx\right|\), or equivalently \(\int_a^c f(x)\,dx + \int_c^b |f(x)|\,dx\), or equivalently \(\int_a^c f(x)\,dx - \int_c^b f(x)\,dx\).

blocks.alt: A curve that is above the x-axis from x = a to x = c (shaded green) and below the axis from x = c to x = b (shaded blue).
blocks.caption: Figure 3.2: the curve is above the axis on [a, c] and below it on [c, b] (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: 3. If \(f(x)\) changes sign at \(c_1, c_2, c_3, \ldots, c_n\) in \((a, b)\) where \(c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_n\) are the roots of \(f(x) = 0\), then

blocks.text_alt: Total area equals the integral from a to b of the absolute value of f of x, which equals the sum of the absolute values of the integrals of f over a to c 1, c 1 to c 2, and so on up to c n to b

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Notes 1 to 3 say one thing: area is always positive, but an integral of a function below the axis is negative. So:
1. Find the roots of \(f(x) = 0\) inside \([a, b]\).
2. Integrate separately on each piece between the roots.
3. Take the absolute value of each piece and add.
If you integrate straight across a root, the positive and negative parts cancel and you get too small an answer.
4. The area bounded by the curve \(x = f(y)\), the \(y\)-axis, the horizontal lines \(y = c\) and \(y = d\) \((d > c)\) is given by \(\int_c^d f(y)\,dy\).

blocks.alt: A region between the y-axis and the curve x = f(y), cut off by the horizontal lines y = c and y = d; the region is shaded.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.3: area between x = f(y) and the y-axis from y = c to y = d (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Here the strips are horizontal: width \(dy\), length \(x = f(y)\). Use this form when the curve is easier to write as \(x\) in terms of \(y\) (for example \(x = 9 - y^2\)) or when the region is bounded by the \(y\)-axis.

5. Area between two curves. If \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous and \(f(x) \ge g(x)\) over the interval \([a, b]\), then the area \(A\) of the region bounded by the graphs of \(f\), \(g\), \(x = a\), and \(x = b\) is

blocks.text_alt: A equals the integral from a to b of f of x minus g of x, d x

blocks.text: The above result does not require \(f(x)\) or \(g(x)\) to remain positive over the interval \([a, b]\).

blocks.alt: Two wavy curves, y = f(x) above and y = g(x) below the x-axis, with the region between them from x = a on the left to x = b on the right shaded.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.4: area between y = f(x) and y = g(x) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed Figure 3.4 the vertical lines are labelled \(x = b\) on the left and \(x = a\) on the right. Since the region runs from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\) with \(a < b\), the left line is \(x = a\) and the right line is \(x = b\), as drawn above.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why does Note 5 work even below the axis? The length of a vertical strip is the distance between the two curves, (upper \(y\)) \(-\) (lower \(y\)). Shifting both curves up or down by the same amount does not change this distance, so the signs of \(f\) and \(g\) themselves do not matter. Only the order matters: \(f\) must be the upper curve.
Signed Area and Net Signed Area
The definite integral \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) gives the area between the curve and the \(x\)-axis, but the interpretation depends on whether the curve crosses the axis.

items: If the entire curve lies above the \(x\)-axis, then the definite integral directly gives the signed area, and it is positive.
If the entire curve lies below the \(x\)-axis, then the definite integral directly gives the signed area, and it is negative.
If some part of the curve is above the axis and some part is below the axis, and we add these areas with their signs (positive for above, negative for below), then we get the net signed area.

blocks.text: Thus:

items: Signed area refers to the case when the curve is entirely above or entirely below the axis.
Net signed area refers to the result after cancelling positive and negative contributions when the curve crosses the axis.

blocks.text: In both cases, the formula is the same:

blocks.text_alt: Signed area, or net signed area, equals the integral from a to b of f of x d x

blocks.text: The result may be:

items: Positive (more area above or entirely above),
Negative (more area below or entirely below), or Zero (equal area above and below).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our own small example: for \(f(x) = x\) on \([-1, 1]\),
\[\int_{-1}^{1} x\,dx = 0\]
so the net signed area is 0 (the triangle above cancels the triangle below). But the total (physical) area is
\[\int_{-1}^{1} |x|\,dx = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\]
When a question says "area", it means the total area; "signed area" means the plain integral.

blocks.title: Example 57
blocks.problem: Find the area bounded by the parabola \(y = x^2 - 5x + 4\) and the \(x\)-axis.
steps:
Given: the parabola \(y = x^2 - 5x + 4\) and the \(x\)-axis.
To find: the area of the region enclosed between them.
Method: find where the parabola meets the \(x\)-axis (these points are the limits), check whether the curve is above or below the axis there, and use Note 1 (take the absolute value) if it is below.

Step 1: \(x\)-intercepts
Set \(y = 0\):
\[x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0\]
\[(x - 1)(x - 4) = 0\]
\[x = 1 \text{ or } x = 4\]
Why: a region "bounded by the curve and the \(x\)-axis" starts and ends where the curve touches the axis, so these roots are the limits of integration.

Step 2: Is the curve above or below the axis?
The parabola opens upwards (leading coefficient \(+1\)). Test \(x = 2\):
\[y(2) = 4 - 10 + 4 = -2 < 0\]
So between \(x = 1\) and \(x = 4\) the curve is below the \(x\)-axis (Figure 3.5).
Why: an upward parabola is negative between its two roots; Note 1 says such an area must be taken with \(|y|\).

Step 3: Set up the integral
\[A = \int_1^4 |y|\,dx\]
\[= \int_1^4 -(x^2 - 5x + 4)\,dx\]
\[= \int_1^4 (-x^2 + 5x - 4)\,dx\]
Why: on \([1, 4]\), \(y \le 0\), so \(|y| = -y\). The minus sign makes every strip height positive.

Step 4: Integrate
\[= \left[-\dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{5x^2}{2} - 4x\right]_1^4\]
Why: power rule \(\int x^n dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\) term by term.

Step 5: Substitute the limits
At \(x = 4\):
\[-\dfrac{64}{3} + \dfrac{80}{2} - 16 = \dfrac{8}{3}\]
At \(x = 1\):
\[-\dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{5}{2} - 4 = -\dfrac{11}{6}\]
\[A = \dfrac{8}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{11}{6}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{16 + 11}{6} = \dfrac{27}{6} = \dfrac{9}{2}\]
Why: Fundamental Theorem: value at the upper limit minus value at the lower limit. Keep the brackets: subtracting a negative number adds it.

Check:
Without the absolute value, \(\int_1^4 (x^2 - 5x + 4)\,dx = -\frac{9}{2}\): negative, as expected for a region below the axis, and of the same size.
Our quick check (not in the book): for a parabola \(y = a(x - \alpha)(x - \beta)\) the area cut off by the axis is \(\frac{|a|}{6}(\beta - \alpha)^3 = \frac{1}{6}(3)^3 = \frac{9}{2}\).

blocks.alt: The parabola y = x squared minus 5x plus 4 crossing the x-axis at (1, 0) and (4, 0), with vertex (2.5, minus 2.25); the region between the curve and the axis is shaded below the axis.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.5: y = x² − 5x + 4 and the x-axis (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Example 58
blocks.problem: Find the area bounded by the curves \(y = 13 - x^2\) and \(y = 2x + 5\).
steps:
Given: the parabola \(y = 13 - x^2\) and the line \(y = 2x + 5\).
To find: the area of the region enclosed between them.
Method: Note 5, area between two curves: find the intersection points (the limits), decide which curve is on top, then integrate (upper \(-\) lower).

Step 1: Points of intersection
\[13 - x^2 = 2x + 5\]
\[8 - x^2 - 2x = 0\]
\[x^2 + 2x - 8 = 0\]
\[(x - 2)(x + 4) = 0\]
\[x = -4 \text{ or } x = 2\]
Points: \(y(2) = 9\), \(y(-4) = -3\), i.e. \((2, 9)\) and \((-4, -3)\).
Why: the enclosed region starts and ends where the two curves meet. The book factorises by splitting \(2x = 4x - 2x\): \(x(x + 4) - 2(x + 4)\).

Step 2: Which curve is on top?
Test \(x = 0\) (inside \([-4, 2]\)):
\[13 - 0^2 = 13, \quad 2(0) + 5 = 5\]
So \(y = 13 - x^2\) is above \(y = 2x + 5\) on \([-4, 2]\).
Why: two continuous curves cannot change order between their meeting points, so one test point is enough.

Step 3: Set up the integral
\[A = \int_{-4}^{2} [\text{upper} - \text{lower}]\,dx\]
\[= \int_{-4}^{2} [(13 - x^2) - (2x + 5)]\,dx\]
\[= \int_{-4}^{2} (8 - x^2 - 2x)\,dx\]
Why: the height of a thin vertical strip is (upper \(y\)) \(-\) (lower \(y\)); this works even where the region goes below the \(x\)-axis.

Step 4: Integrate
\[= \left[8x - \dfrac{x^3}{3} - x^2\right]_{-4}^{2}\]
Why: power rule term by term.

Step 5: Substitute the limits
At \(x = 2\):
\[16 - \dfrac{8}{3} - 4 = \dfrac{28}{3}\]
At \(x = -4\):
\[-32 + \dfrac{64}{3} - 16 = -\dfrac{80}{3}\]
\[A = \dfrac{28}{3} + \dfrac{80}{3} = \dfrac{108}{3} = 36\]
The book groups the same numbers as \(60 - \left(\frac{8}{3} + \frac{64}{3}\right) = 60 - 24 = 36\).
Why: \(-(-4)^3 = +64\), so \(-\frac{(-4)^3}{3} = +\frac{64}{3}\); watch the signs with negative limits.

Check:
Our quick check: the strip height \(8 - 2x - x^2 = -(x - 2)(x + 4)\) is a parabola with \(|a| = 1\), so the area is \(\frac{1}{6}(2 - (-4))^3 = \frac{216}{6} = 36\). It agrees.
blocks.answer: The area between the two curves is 36 square units.

blocks.caption: Figure 3.6: y = 13 − x² and y = 2x + 5 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Example 59
blocks.problem: Find the area of the region bounded by the parabolas \(y = 4 - x^2\) and \(y = x^2 - 2x\).
steps:
Given: the parabolas \(y = 4 - x^2\) (opens down) and \(y = x^2 - 2x\) (opens up).
To find: the area of the region enclosed between them.
Method: area between two curves (Note 5): intersection points, the upper curve, then \(\int (f - g)\,dx\).

Step 1: Points of intersection
\[4 - x^2 = x^2 - 2x\]
\[-2x^2 + 2x + 4 = 0\]
Divide by \(-2\):
\[x^2 - x - 2 = 0\]
\[(x + 1)(x - 2) = 0\]
\[x = -1 \text{ or } x = 2\]
Points: \((-1, 3)\) and \((2, 0)\).
Why: the region is closed off where the two parabolas meet.

Step 2: Which curve is on top?
Take \(x = 0 \in [-1, 2]\):
\[y = 4 - 0^2 = 4, \quad y = 0^2 - 2(0) = 0\]
So \(f(x) = 4 - x^2\) is the upper curve and \(g(x) = x^2 - 2x\) the lower curve.

Step 3: Set up and integrate
\[A = \int_{-1}^{2} [f(x) - g(x)]\,dx\]
\[= \int_{-1}^{2} [(4 - x^2) - (x^2 - 2x)]\,dx\]
\[= \int_{-1}^{2} (4 - 2x^2 + 2x)\,dx\]
\[= \left[4x - \dfrac{2}{3}x^3 + x^2\right]_{-1}^{2}\]
Why: remove the brackets carefully: \(-(x^2 - 2x) = -x^2 + 2x\).

Check:
Our quick check: \(f - g = -2(x + 1)(x - 2)\) has \(|a| = 2\), so the area is \(\frac{2}{6}(3)^3 = 9\). It agrees.

blocks.alt: The parabolas y = 4 minus x squared and y = x squared minus 2x meeting at (minus 1, 3) and (2, 0); the region between them is shaded.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.7: y = 4 − x² and y = x² − 2x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Area under \(y = f(x) \ge 0\) from \(a\) to \(b\): \(A = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).
2. Below the axis, take the absolute value: \(A = \left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\right|\).
3. If the curve crosses the axis, split at the roots and add the absolute values of the pieces.
4. Between two curves: \(A = \int_a^b [\text{upper} - \text{lower}]\,dx\), limits from the intersection points.
5. Horizontal strips: \(A = \int_c^d x\,dy\) for a region against the \(y\)-axis.
6. Signed area = the plain integral; it can be positive, negative or zero. Total area is never negative.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Integrating straight across a root: \(\int_{-3}^{3} (x^2 - 4)\,dx = -6\) is the net signed area, not the total area \(\frac{46}{3}\).
2. Writing (lower \(-\) upper) and getting a negative area; always test a point to see which curve is on top.
3. Removing brackets wrongly: \(-(x^2 - 2x) = -x^2 + 2x\), not \(-x^2 - 2x\).
4. Sign slips with negative limits, such as \((-4)^3 = -64\).
